chapters.title: models.py
chapters.subtitle: Fields, relationships, constraints and validation
chapters.summary: How to shape the database in Python: the right field, the right relationship, the constraint that protects the invariant, and the validation that runs before save.
chapters.quick_answer: A model class maps to a table and each field maps to a column. Choose the narrowest field that expresses the data, set `on_delete` deliberately, add database constraints for invariants, and put reusable validation in `clean()` rather than only in forms.

sections.title: A model is a table with a Python face
sections.body:
Each concrete model becomes a table. Each field becomes a column. Django adds an `id` primary key unless you declare one. `Meta` carries table-level behaviour: ordering, constraints, indexes, verbose names.

`__str__` is not cosmetic: it is what the admin, shell and logs show. Give every model a useful one.
sections.code:
from django.db import models

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    body = models.TextField()
    published_at = models.DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)

    class Meta:
        ordering = ["-published_at", "-created_at"]
        indexes = [models.Index(fields=["slug"])]

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title

sections.title: Choose the narrowest field
sections.body:
The field type is documentation, validation and database type at once. Do not use `CharField` for everything.

- `CharField(max_length=...)` — short text with a hard limit.
- `TextField()` — long text; no database length limit.
- `EmailField()` — email validation on top of `CharField`.
- `SlugField()` — URL-safe letters, numbers, hyphens, underscores.
- `IntegerField`, `PositiveIntegerField`, `DecimalField` — numbers; `DecimalField` needs `max_digits` and `decimal_places`.
- `BooleanField(default=False)` — never use `null=True` for a boolean.
- `DateField`, `DateTimeField` — dates; `auto_now_add` sets once, `auto_now` updates every save.
- `JSONField()` — structured data when the shape is genuinely flexible.
sections.code:
price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=8, decimal_places=2)
stock = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)
is_active = models.BooleanField(default=True)
metadata = models.JSONField(default=dict, blank=True)
sections.note: `null=True` controls the database; `blank=True` controls form validation. They are not synonyms.

sections.title: Relationships and on_delete
sections.body:
`ForeignKey` is many-to-one, `ManyToManyField` is many-to-many, `OneToOneField` is a unique one-to-one. `on_delete` is required on `ForeignKey` and `OneToOneField` because the database must decide what happens to children when the parent disappears.

- `CASCADE` — delete children too. Correct for owned rows.
- `PROTECT` — refuse the delete. Correct for important references.
- `SET_NULL` — keep the child; requires `null=True`.
- `SET_DEFAULT` — replace with a default.
- `DO_NOTHING` — almost always a mistake; it can leave dangling rows.

`related_name` names the reverse accessor: `author.posts.all()`.

sections.title: Constraints are promises the database keeps
sections.body:
Application validation can be bypassed by a script, a bulk update or a race. Database constraints hold even then. Use `UniqueConstraint` for multi-column uniqueness and `CheckConstraint` for ranges and state rules.

Catch `IntegrityError` at the boundary and turn it into a form error; do not hide it with a bare `except`.
sections.note: On Django 5.1+ `CheckConstraint` uses `condition=`. Older code may use `check=`; follow the version you deploy.

sections.title: Validation belongs in the model too
sections.body:
`full_clean()` runs field validation, `clean_fields()`, `clean()` and constraint checks. `save()` does not call `full_clean()` automatically; forms do. If a model can be created from a script, a command or an API, call `full_clean()` in the service layer or override `save()` carefully.

Put cross-field invariants in `clean()` and raise `ValidationError` with a field key when possible.
sections.note: Overriding `save()` to call `full_clean()` is a trade-off: it adds a query per save and can surprise bulk operations. Many teams call `full_clean()` explicitly in services instead.

sections.title: Custom user: decide before the first migrate
sections.body:
The default `User` is fine for a prototype. If you need email login, a different identifier or extra fields, create a custom user before the first migration. Swapping it later requires a careful data migration and is a common source of pain.

Extend `AbstractUser` when you want the built-in fields; extend `AbstractBaseUser` only when you need full control. Point `AUTH_USER_MODEL` at the model and reference it with `get_user_model()` or `settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL`.
sections.code:
# accounts/models.py
from django.contrib.auth.models import AbstractUser
from django.db import models

class User(AbstractUser):
    email = models.EmailField(unique=True)
    display_name = models.CharField(max_length=80, blank=True)

# settings.py
AUTH_USER_MODEL = "accounts.User"

# anywhere else
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
User = get_user_model()
sections.note: Do not import the concrete user model directly in reusable apps; use `get_user_model()`.

pitfalls: Using `null=True` on `CharField` and creating two empty states (`NULL` and `""`).
Using `CASCADE` for a reference that should survive the parent; use `PROTECT` or `SET_NULL`.
Forgetting `related_name` and then guessing the reverse accessor.
Relying only on form validation for an invariant that scripts and APIs can bypass.
Adding a custom user after `migrate` has created `auth.User`.
checklist: Every field is the narrowest type that fits.
Every relationship has a deliberate `on_delete` and a useful `related_name`.
Invariants have database constraints where possible.
Custom user decision made before the first migration.

chapters.title: Migrations
chapters.subtitle: Schema history you can review, apply and reverse
chapters.summary: Migrations are version-controlled Python files that describe schema changes. Learn the loop, the data-migration pattern, and how to recover without guessing.
chapters.quick_answer: Change the model, run `makemigrations`, review the generated file, then run `migrate`. Commit migrations. Use `RunPython` for data changes and never edit an already-applied migration.

sections.title: The loop
sections.body:
`makemigrations` compares models to the migration history and writes new files. `migrate` applies them to the database and records what ran. The migration files are the source of truth; the database is a consumer.

Always read the generated file. Check the field type, defaults, nullability and any data operation. A migration that runs instantly on 100 rows can lock a table for minutes on 10 million.
sections.code:
python manage.py makemigrations
python manage.py makemigrations blog --name add_post_status
python manage.py sqlmigrate blog 0003
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py showmigrations blog

sections.title: What a migration file contains
sections.body:
A migration has dependencies, operations and an optional `RunPython`. Dependencies tell Django what must run first. Operations are reversible where possible.

Do not edit a migration that has already been applied in an environment you care about. Add a new migration instead. If nobody has applied it yet, deleting and regenerating is safe.
sections.code:
from django.db import migrations, models

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [("blog", "0002_post_slug")]

    operations = [
        migrations.AddField(
            model_name="post",
            name="status",
            field=models.CharField(
                max_length=12,
                choices=[("draft", "Draft"), ("published", "Published")],
                default="draft",
            ),
        ),
    ]

sections.title: Data migrations
sections.body:
Schema migrations change tables. Data migrations change rows. Use `RunPython` with two functions: forwards and backwards. Always use the historical model from `apps.get_model()`; importing the live model couples the migration to future code.

For large tables, batch the work and make the migration idempotent. A migration that times out halfway is much easier to recover when it can be re-run.
sections.note: Use `migrations.RunPython.noop` when a data migration genuinely has no safe reverse.

sections.title: Rollback, fake and recovery
sections.body:
`migrate blog 0002` unapplies migrations after `0002` for that app. It is a schema rollback, not a backup: data added by later migrations may be lost. In production, prefer a new forward migration over a rollback.

`--fake` records a migration as applied without running it. It is for recovering from a known drift, not for skipping a failed migration. `--fake-initial` is for adopting an existing database into a project with an initial migration.
sections.code:
python manage.py migrate blog 0002
python manage.py migrate blog 0004 --fake
python manage.py migrate --fake-initial
python manage.py showmigrations --plan
sections.note: Before any manual migration surgery, take a database backup. A migration mistake is recoverable; a deleted table is not.

sections.title: Zero-downtime habits
sections.body:
During a rolling deploy, old and new code run at the same time. A migration must therefore be compatible with both versions.

The safe pattern is expand → migrate → contract: add nullable columns or new tables, deploy code that writes both shapes, backfill in batches, then remove the old shape in a later release. Avoid adding a non-nullable column without a default to a large table, and avoid renaming a column in one step.
sections.code:
# Release 1: add the new nullable column
# Release 2: deploy code that writes old and new
# Release 3: backfill in batches, then add the constraint
# Release 4: remove the old column

pitfalls: Editing a migration that is already applied in staging or production.
Deleting migration files and recreating them while the database still has the old history.
Importing live models inside a data migration instead of `apps.get_model()`.
Running `migrate --fake` to make an error disappear without understanding the drift.
Adding a non-nullable field without a default to a large table in one step.
checklist: Generated migration reviewed, not blindly committed.
Data migrations use historical models and are reversible.
Migration files committed with the model change.
Production plan accounts for old and new code overlapping.
A database backup exists before destructive changes.

chapters.title: ORM & QuerySets
chapters.subtitle: Queries, joins, aggregation and the N+1 trap
chapters.summary: How to get the data you need in the number of queries you expect: lookups, joins, prefetching, aggregation, transactions and the N+1 diagnosis.
chapters.quick_answer: QuerySets are lazy; they hit the database when you iterate, slice with a step, call `len()`, `list()`, `count()` or `exists()`. Use `select_related` for foreign keys and one-to-one, `prefetch_related` for many-to-many and reverse relations, and inspect `connection.queries` when a page feels slow.

sections.title: QuerySets are lazy
sections.body:
Building a QuerySet does not run SQL. Chaining filters builds a query description. The database is hit when the result is needed.

This is why a QuerySet can be passed around and refined, and why a loop over a QuerySet inside a template can quietly run one query per row. Evaluate once, then reuse the list if the result is needed more than once.
sections.code:
posts = Post.objects.filter(published=True)  # no query yet
posts = posts.order_by("-published_at")      # still no query
for post in posts:                           # query runs here
    print(post.title)

# Force evaluation once when you need the same rows repeatedly:
posts = list(Post.objects.filter(published=True))

sections.title: Lookups cover most SQL you need
sections.body:
Field lookups use `__`: `__exact`, `__iexact`, `__contains`, `__icontains`, `__in`, `__gt`, `__gte`, `__lt`, `__lte`, `__startswith`, `__isnull`, `__range`, `__year`, `__date`. Related fields use the same double underscore: `author__email`.

`Q` objects combine conditions with `&`, `|` and `~`. `F` refers to another column and lets the database do arithmetic atomically.
sections.code:
from django.db.models import F, Q

Post.objects.filter(title__icontains="django")
Post.objects.filter(status__in=["draft", "review"])
Post.objects.filter(published_at__isnull=True)
Post.objects.filter(author__email__iendswith="@example.com")
Post.objects.filter(Q(status="draft") | Q(published_at__isnull=True))
Post.objects.filter(view_count__gte=F("like_count"))
Post.objects.filter(created_at__year=2026)

sections.title: Joins, prefetching and the N+1 trap
sections.body:
`select_related` performs a SQL join and is for `ForeignKey` and `OneToOneField`. `prefetch_related` runs a second query and joins in Python; it is for `ManyToManyField` and reverse relations. Both reduce queries, but only when the related data is actually used.

The N+1 problem: one query for 50 posts, then 50 queries for each author. The page works, then gets slower as the data grows. Fix it at the queryset, not in the template.
sections.code:
# 1 query for posts + 1 for authors
posts = Post.objects.select_related("author").all()

# 1 query for posts + 1 for tags
posts = Post.objects.prefetch_related("tags").all()

# Custom prefetch with a filtered queryset
from django.db.models import Prefetch
posts = Post.objects.prefetch_related(
    Prefetch("comments", queryset=Comment.objects.filter(approved=True), to_attr="approved_comments")
)

# Diagnose
from django.db import connection
print(len(connection.queries))
sections.note: `select_related` on a reverse `ForeignKey` raises `FieldError`; use `prefetch_related` for the reverse side.

sections.title: Aggregation and annotation
sections.body:
`aggregate()` returns one dictionary for the whole queryset. `annotate()` adds a computed value per row. Use `Count`, `Sum`, `Avg`, `Min`, `Max` and `F` expressions; let the database do the work.

Watch for double counting when you annotate across multiple many-to-many relations. `Count(..., distinct=True)` is often necessary.
sections.code:
from django.db.models import Avg, Count, Sum

Post.objects.aggregate(total=Count("id"), avg_views=Avg("view_count"))

Author.objects.annotate(
    post_count=Count("posts", distinct=True),
    total_views=Sum("posts__view_count"),
).order_by("-total_views")[:10]

sections.title: Transactions and bulk operations
sections.body:
Wrap a group of writes that must succeed or fail together in `transaction.atomic()`. If an exception escapes, the block rolls back. Do not catch an exception inside the block and continue writing unless you understand the transaction state.

`bulk_create` and `bulk_update` are much faster than a loop of `save()` calls, but they bypass `save()` and signals. Use them for imports and backfills, not as a default.
sections.code:
from django.db import transaction

with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.create(customer=customer)
    for item in items:
        OrderItem.objects.create(order=order, **item)

# Atomic stock decrement without a read-modify-write race
Product.objects.filter(pk=product.pk, stock__gte=quantity).update(
    stock=F("stock") - quantity
)

Post.objects.bulk_create([Post(title=t) for t in titles], batch_size=500)

sections.title: When the query is the problem
sections.body:
Measure before optimising. `QuerySet.explain()` shows the database plan. `only()` and `defer()` limit columns, but can cause extra queries when deferred fields are accessed later. `iterator()` streams large result sets without loading everything into memory.

Add indexes for columns used in filters, ordering and joins. A missing index on a foreign key is a common slow query; Django creates one automatically for `ForeignKey`, but not for every filtered field.

pitfalls: Calling `len(queryset)` repeatedly instead of evaluating once.
Using `select_related` for many-to-many data; it raises an error or creates a huge join.
Annotating multiple relations without `distinct=True` and double-counting.
Catching an exception inside `transaction.atomic()` and continuing to write.
Using `bulk_create` and expecting `save()` or `post_save` to run.
checklist: The page's query count is known and stable.
Foreign keys used in templates are selected or prefetched.
Aggregates happen in the database, not in Python loops.
Large exports and imports use batching or streaming.
